title: Count Below
statement:
A box starts empty. You process `q` events in order. Event `1 x` puts a ball numbered `x` into the box (the same number may be added many times). Event `2 x` asks how many balls currently in the box have a number less than or equal to `x`.

**Input.** First line: `M` and `q`. Then `q` lines `t x`, with `t` equal to `1` or `2` and `1 ≤ x ≤ M`.

**Output.** For every event of type `2`, in order, print the answer on its own line.
constraints: 1 ≤ M ≤ 100000, 1 ≤ q ≤ 20000 in this browser version (the idea scales to 2·10^5 and beyond)
at least one event of type 2
hints: Keeping a count array makes insertion O(1) but a query would add up to M cells. Keeping prefix counts makes a query O(1) but an insertion touches up to M cells.
Store, at index i, the count of the last (i & -i) positions ending at i. A prefix is then the sum of O(log M) such blocks.
To insert at x, add 1 at x, then x += x & -x until you pass M. To query up to x, add bit[x], then x -= x & -x until x is 0.
editorial: A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) keeps `bit[i]`, the sum of the `i & -i` elements ending at `i`, where `i & -i` is the lowest set bit of `i`. A prefix sum walks down by removing the lowest set bit each step, visiting at most `log M` nodes. A point update walks up by adding the lowest set bit, touching at most `log M` nodes that cover `x`. Counting balls `<= x` is a prefix sum over a count array, so both events cost `O(log M)`. A plain array would make one of the two operations `O(M)`, which is too slow at the real limits. Fenwick trees are shorter than segment trees but only support operations with an inverse (such as sums), not min or max.

starter.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
M, q = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
# events start at data[2]: t x

solutions.python:
import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
M, q = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
bit = [0] * (M + 1)           # bit[i] covers the last (i & -i) positions ending at i
out = []
for i in range(q):
    t, x = int(data[2 + 2 * i]), int(data[3 + 2 * i])
    if t == 1:
        while x <= M:
            bit[x] += 1
            x += x & -x       # climb to the next node that covers x
    else:
        s = 0
        while x > 0:
            s += bit[x]
            x -= x & -x       # drop the lowest set bit
        out.append(s)
print("\n".join(map(str, out)))
